enum { MISS, HIT, CRITICALHIT }

\\\ A pool of enum outcomes may have any dimension. It cannot be summed, but it
\\\ can be iterated over its multisets, which is what an `s` parameter does.
function: hits SEQ:s { result: [count {HIT, CRITICALHIT} in SEQ] }
output [hits 3d{MISS, HIT, CRITICALHIT}] named "hits per multiset"

\\\ Multisets are sorted by declaration order, and "position order" chooses which
\\\ end comes first. Selecting a single position is the only way to see this,
\\\ since enum members support no ordering comparisons of their own.
function: first SEQ:s { result: 1@SEQ }
output [first 3d{MISS, HIT}] named "best of three"
set "position order" to "lowest first"
output [first 3d{MISS, HIT}] named "worst of three"
set "position order" to "highest first"

\\\ `count` and `contains` take the pool itself rather than its multisets, so
\\\ they neither sum nor enumerate it. This pool has 888030 multisets; going
\\\ through Icepool keeps it instant.
enum { FA, FB, FC, FD, FE, FF, FG, FH }
LARGE: 20d{FA, FB, FC, FD, FE, FF, FG, FH}
output [count {FA} in LARGE] named "count over a large pool"
output [LARGE contains FA] named "contains over a large pool"

\\\ An empty pool has nothing to add, so it is summable at any dimension.
output 2d{MISS:0} named "empty at dimension two"

output #(2d(2d{MISS, HIT})) named "dimension"
